title: Luciano de San-Saor: the Telephone Operator, Mujeres Libres, and Thirty Years of Being Nobody
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: Peñuelas, and the Name She Takes

stops.name: Pozal de Gallinas, the father's village
stops.date_confidence: undated in the sources; the date is a placeholder set before her birth to order the segment. es.wikipedia attaches Pozal de Gallinas specifically to her father, Eugenio Sánchez Rodríguez; that her mother also came from there is not stated anywhere consulted. The framing of a general wave of rural migration is the writer's gloss, not a sourced claim.
stops.campa: Two hundred kilometres northwest of Madrid, in the flat wheat country of Valladolid province, is the village her father leaves. Pozal de Gallinas sends its young to the capital the way the Castilian villages do in those decades, into the tenement barrios going up south of the river and into whatever work the yards and the workshops have. Eugenio Sánchez Rodríguez carries his surname to Madrid. The second name, the one she will sign for fifty years, is her mother's, and where Gabriela Saornil Serrano came from no source consulted says.
suggested_refs: Pozal de Gallinas, Valladolid province, the paternal village

stops.name: Peñuelas, Madrid, the birth on Calle del Labrador
stops.date_confidence: attested. Birth date, parents and the Peñuelas address are given by es.wikipedia; the deaths of her brother José (1900), her sister Eleuteria (1901) and her mother (1908) are attested separately and folded into this stop.
stops.campa: In the Peñuelas quarter, on Calle del Labrador, a daughter is born to Eugenio Sánchez Rodríguez and Gabriela Saornil Serrano, in a barrio built out of the countryside's overflow. The house does not keep what it is given. Her brother José dies in 1900, her sister Eleuteria at a year old in 1901, her mother in 1908, and Lucía, twelve, takes on the running of what is left: a father, a surviving sister, a wage that has to come from somewhere. The poems come later. The arithmetic comes first.
suggested_refs: The Peñuelas quarter of Madrid, working-class Arganzuela, in the 1890s

stops.name: Centro Hijos de Madrid, the Casa de los Gatos
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1913 by es.wikipedia; the month is not given and defaults to January. That the Centro was one of very few routes to instruction open to a girl of her class is a reconstruction, not a sourced statement.
stops.campa: She enrols at the Centro Hijos de Madrid, the working-class institute the city calls the Casa de los Gatos, and studies painting there alongside whatever else the curriculum will give her, while holding a job because the household needs the money. It is not a university and she will never see one. It is what is open to a girl of the Peñuelas who reads well past what she is taught. She stays with the painting long enough that forty years later she can put it on a form as her trade.
suggested_refs: The Centro Hijos de Madrid, popularly the Casa de los Gatos, and its evening instruction

stops.name: Ciudad Rodrigo, the first poem in Avante
stops.date_confidence: attested to January 1914; the day is not given. She is living in Madrid and there is no record of her ever visiting Ciudad Rodrigo. The pin marks where the poem is printed, not where she stands.
stops.campa: A weekly called Avante, printed in a walled border town in Salamanca province she has never seen, sets her first poem in type. It is called 'Nieve.' She is eighteen. A girl from the Peñuelas with no money and no literary connections finds a printer four hundred kilometres away who will take verse from anyone who posts it, and posts. Almost everything that follows will work the same way, out through the provincial press, in envelopes, under names not on her birth certificate. She never sets foot in Ciudad Rodrigo.
sources: Spanish Wikipedia, 'Lucía Sánchez Saornil' (Avante, Ciudad Rodrigo, January 1914)
suggested_refs: Avante, weekly of Ciudad Rodrigo, issue carrying 'Nieve,' January 1914

stops.name: Madrid, the switchboard
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1916 by both language Wikipedias; the month is not given and defaults to January. The exact exchange building is not identified in the sources and the pin is central Madrid.
stops.campa: She takes work as an operator at the Compañía Madrileña de Teléfonos, the firm that will become Telefónica, joining the first Spanish generation of women paid a wage to sit at a board and connect strangers to each other. The hours are long and the discipline is exact, and it is here rather than in any hall that her politics are made. She will hold the job fifteen years, be promoted to first class, be transferred to Valencia and back, and walk out of it before the strike that everyone remembers her for.
suggested_refs: The Compañía Madrileña de Teléfonos and the feminisation of the Spanish switchboard trade

stops.name: Madrid, Los Quijotes and the name Luciano de San-Saor
stops.date_confidence: 1916 attested for the first collaborations with Los Quijotes and for the pseudonym; the month is not given and is set mid-year to order the segment. es.wikipedia gives the out-of-Madrid publishing period as 1916-1918 without assigning individual years, and names Cádiz-San Fernando as a periodical, not a place.
stops.campa: She begins publishing in the Madrid magazine Los Quijotes under a man's name, Luciano de San-Saor, assembled out of her own two surnames. Between 1916 and 1918 that name also places verse outside the capital, principally in the periodical Cádiz-San Fernando, and in El Progreso de Lugo, and in the collection Los Noveles. Editors correspond with a promising young man. She keeps the name for most of her literary life. Not one of the writers who answer his letters is on record as having asked who he was.
suggested_refs: Los Quijotes (Madrid, 1915-1918), and the signature Luciano de San-Saor

stops.name: Seville, the ultraístas and the magazine Grecia
stops.date_confidence: attested: January 1919 for her adhesion to ultraísmo and her poems in Grecia, and 31 December 1919 for Borges's first poem in the same magazine, which is attested on borges.journey.json. No meeting between the two is attested anywhere; what is attested is a shared movement and a shared masthead.
stops.campa: Grecia, edited out of Seville, opens the ultraísta movement to her, and from January 1919 her poems run in it and in Cervantes, Ultra, Tableros and Vértices. She is the movement's only woman of any standing, and the movement does not know it. On the last day of that year the same magazine prints a first poem by a nineteen-year-old Argentine passing through Spain, Jorge Luis Borges. Two writers who will each be read for a century share a masthead. Neither is recorded as having met the other.
sources: Spanish Wikipedia, 'Lucía Sánchez Saornil' (ultraísmo, Grecia, January 1919)
suggested_refs: Grecia (Seville, 1918-1920), the founding organ of ultraísmo

stops.name: Café Colonial, Madrid, the table she is a name at
stops.date_confidence: the Café Colonial tertulia of Rafael Cansinos-Assens is attested for February 1920 on borges.journey.json. Sánchez Saornil's own attendance is not attested in any source consulted; her presence in the movement's magazines is. The stop reports the gap rather than filling it.
stops.campa: On Saturday nights Rafael Cansinos-Assens holds court at the Café Colonial and the ultraístas argue their manifestos into shape over the marble. Luciano de San-Saor is a name in that room, printed, discussed, counted among the signatories of the movement. An operator finishing a shift at the interurban centre keeps different hours from a café poet, and a woman in Madrid in 1920 has a different set of doors. Whether the woman who owns the name ever sat down at that table, no source consulted says.
suggested_refs: Rafael Cansinos-Assens's Saturday tertulia at the Café Colonial, Madrid

stops.name: Madrid, Plural, and the years after ultraísmo
stops.date_confidence: attested: Plural (1925) closes her strictly ultraísta phase, the movement itself having wound down around 1923; es.wikipedia has her continuing in Manantial (1929) and La Gaceta Literaria (1930-1931), so 1925 is not the end of her periodical writing. Months are not given and default to January.
stops.campa: Ultraísmo burns out around 1923 and she closes her strictly ultraísta account with poems in Plural in 1925. She does not stop. Manantial takes her in 1929, La Gaceta Literaria in 1930 and 1931. By the time the last of these appears she has been publishing for seventeen years and no reader has met her. Then the literary byline thins and goes out, and the writing that replaces it is signed La Compañera X, Vigía, El Observador, and set in the columns of a union daily. No manifesto marks the crossing.
suggested_refs: Plural (1925), Manantial (1929), La Gaceta Literaria (1930-1931)

stops.name: Valencia, transferred by the company
stops.date_confidence: attested: promotion to first-class operator at the Madrid-Alcalá interurban centre in March 1927, transfer to Valencia in September 1927. The day is not given.
stops.campa: In March she is made a first-class operator at the Madrid-Alcalá interurban centre, running the long-distance lines out of the capital; in September the company moves her to Valencia on service requirements. It is her first long residence away from Madrid, it is not political, and she is not yet anything the state would keep a file on. She will come back to Valencia twice, in 1937 and in 1948. The second time she stays twenty-two years and dies here.
suggested_refs: Telefónica personnel records for the Madrid-Alcalá interurban centre, 1927

stops.name: Madrid, out of the company
stops.date_confidence: attested to 29 January 1931 by es.wikipedia. The order matters and is commonly reported backwards: this is before the Republic is proclaimed on 14 April and before the July telephone strike, so it cannot be a consequence of either, and it is not final, since she is readmitted to the company in October 1936. Her membership of Balbontín's Partido Radical Socialista Revolucionario, abandoned in 1932, is often miscited as the Partido Republicano Radical Socialista, a different organisation.
stops.campa: She leaves the Compañía Telefónica Nacional on the twenty-ninth of January, ten weeks before the Republic is proclaimed and six months before the strike that most accounts credit with pushing her out. The sequence is the opposite of the legend: she is already gone when the confrontation comes, and she returns to it as a militant rather than an employee. Her party membership, in José Antonio Balbontín's Partido Radical Socialista Revolucionario, she will drop the following year and never replace with another.
sources: Spanish Wikipedia, 'Lucía Sánchez Saornil' (baja 29 January 1931; readmitted October 1936)
suggested_refs: Telefónica staff register, entry of 29 January 1931

stops.name: Madrid, the telephone strike
stops.date_confidence: the CNT-led national telephone strike runs from July 1931 and her brief detention is attested; no exact date is given for the arrest and the day here is a placeholder within the month.
stops.campa: The CNT calls the telephone workers out against the company in July and the young Republic answers with police. She is in it, six months off the payroll and with nothing to lose but her liberty, and she is arrested and held briefly. Three months old, the Republic is policing a strike the way the monarchy policed strikes. Whatever remained of her parliamentary politics does not survive the cell. Five years later the same company will take her back, in October 1936, with the war on and the workers running it.
suggested_refs: The CNT telephone strike of July 1931 and its repression under the Republic

stops.name: Madrid, the Sindicato Nacional de Teléfonos, member 26
stops.date_confidence: 1931 attested for the CNT affiliation and for the membership number 26; the month is not given and is set at year's end to order the segment. The Fanelli mission is the standard account of the doctrine's arrival in Spain and is attested on mikhail_bakunin.journey.json for the founding of the Alliance in 1868; Bakunin died in 1876 and the relation is doctrinal descent, not acquaintance.
stops.campa: Her card in the CNT's national telephone syndicate carries the number 26. The confederation she is joining was seeded sixty years earlier by Giuseppe Fanelli, sent into Spain by Mikhail Bakunin with no Spanish and a doctrine that took anyway: no state, no parliament, no waiting. It is by now the largest anarcho-syndicalist movement on earth, and it has almost nothing to say about the women inside it. She joins knowing that. The argument she is about to start is with her own side.
sources: Spanish Wikipedia, 'Lucía Sánchez Saornil' (CNT Sindicato Nacional de Teléfonos, no. 26, 1931)
mikhail_bakunin.journey.json (the 1868 Alliance and the Spanish correspondence)
suggested_refs: The CNT Sindicato Nacional de Teléfonos membership roll, 1931

stops.name: Cuenca, the circuit of halls
stops.date_confidence: es.wikipedia gives 1932-1933 as a single range for the whole rally circuit and assigns no town its own year; the date here orders the segment and is not attested for Cuenca specifically. The list of towns is explicitly non-exhaustive in the source. The portrait of her as a speaker is paraphrased from Martha Ackelsberg, Free Women of Spain, p. 122, which reports what surviving comrades recalled in interview.
stops.campa: Through 1932 and 1933 she speaks at meetings in Cuenca, Manzanares, León, Burgos, La Horra, Talavera de la Reina and Madrid, and the source that lists them ends with an etcetera, which means nobody counted. She is a small woman and, by the account her surviving comrades gave Martha Ackelsberg decades later, diffident until she stands up. Then she is the one who sums up the discussion and the room follows her. They kept comparing her, in build and in temperament, to Louise Michel.
sources: Martha Ackelsberg, Free Women of Spain (AK Press), p. 122
suggested_refs: CNT meeting notices in the provincial libertarian press, 1932-1933

stops.name: Burgos, the argument in the hall
stops.date_confidence: same 1932-1933 range as the rest of the circuit; the month and year here order the segment and are not attested for Burgos specifically. On the aside: Burgos became the rebel seat of government in July 1936 and Franco's wartime capital from January 1938, three to five years after the rally, not six as is sometimes written.
stops.campa: She puts the case in Burgos: that the emancipation of women is not a reward to be handed out once the revolution has succeeded, but a condition of its succeeding at all. She is thirty-seven, attached to no party since she dropped Balbontín's the year before, speaking as an anarchist to anarchists. Three years later the generals will make this city the seat of their Junta de Defensa Nacional, and from January 1938 Franco's wartime capital. Nothing in the hall in 1933 announces it. No text of what she said that night was taken down.
suggested_refs: Burgos as rebel capital, July 1936 to 1939

segments.name: The Question in Our Own Ranks

stops.name: Retiro Park, Madrid, the bench
stops.date_confidence: 1933 attested for the CNT meeting at which the two women were talked over and for the conversation that followed; the month is not given and defaults to order the segment. The Retiro setting comes from English Wikipedia, following Ackelsberg.
stops.campa: At a CNT meeting the men talk over the two women who try to speak, and Lucía Sánchez Saornil and Mercedes Comaposada walk out together into the Retiro. On a bench there they work out what will take three more years to build: not a women's section of the confederation, answerable to it, but an autonomous organisation of women, which is a different proposition and one the confederation will resist for as long as both exist. Amparo Poch y Gascón, a doctor from Zaragoza, makes the third.
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Lucía Sánchez Saornil' (1933 CNT meeting; the Retiro conversation with Comaposada)
Martha Ackelsberg, Free Women of Spain
suggested_refs: The Parque del Retiro, Madrid, autumn 1933

stops.name: Madrid, jefa de redacción at the daily CNT
stops.date_confidence: 1933 attested for her work heading the editorial department of the daily CNT and for the pseudonyms La Compañera X, Vigía and El Observador; the month is not given and orders the segment. The exact address of the paper's offices is not identified in the sources and the pin is central Madrid.
stops.campa: She runs the editorial desk of the anarchist daily CNT, one of very few women setting copy for the confederation's own press, and she writes into her own paper as La Compañera X, as Vigía, as El Observador. The pseudonyms are no longer literary cover. They are the ordinary equipment of a movement that expects to be prosecuted, and they let one writer appear in three registers on a single page. By now she has been signing names not her own for seventeen years, and she has another thirty to go.
suggested_refs: The daily CNT (Madrid), 1933-1934, and the columns signed La Compañera X

stops.name: Madrid, the first of the articles in Solidaridad Obrera
stops.date_confidence: es.wikipedia places the series in Solidaridad Obrera in the autumn of 1935 under the title 'La cuestión femenina en nuestros medios'; the dates of individual articles are not given and 15 September orders the segment. English Wikipedia names FAI's Tierra y Libertad as an additional venue; es.wikipedia does not corroborate it and the contradiction is left open.
stops.campa: In the autumn she publishes a series in Solidaridad Obrera under the title 'The Woman Question in Our Ranks,' and the ranks in question are her own. She writes that comrades who denounce property are proprietary about their wives; that the cult of the mother has been allowed to swallow the woman whole, the function annulling the individual; that the supposed inferiority of women may have cost civilisation centuries. None of it is aimed at the Church or the bourgeoisie. It is aimed at the men in the hall.
stops.quote: The supposed 'inferiority of women.' A mistaken notion that may well have set civilization back by centuries.
stops.quote_source: Lucía Sánchez Saornil, 'La cuestión femenina en nuestros medios,' Solidaridad Obrera, autumn 1935, trans. Paul Sharkey
sources: Lucía Sánchez Saornil, 'La cuestión femenina en nuestros medios,' Solidaridad Obrera, September-October 1935, trans. Paul Sharkey, in Robert Graham, ed., Anarchism: A Documentary History of Libertarian Ideas, vol. 1; excerpted at libcom.org
suggested_refs: Solidaridad Obrera, 15 October 1935, on the concept of the mother absorbing that of the woman

stops.name: Madrid, the answer to Mariano R. Vázquez
stops.date_confidence: the exchange with Vázquez is attested within the 1935 series; individual article dates are not given and the day orders the segment. Rank matters: Vázquez heads the CNT's Catalan regional committee at this point and becomes national general secretary only in November 1936, so he must not be called general secretary in 1935.
stops.campa: Mariano R. Vázquez, who runs the CNT in Catalonia and will run it nationally within a year, sets out the confederation's position on the liberation of women, and she answers him in print, by name, in the confederation's own paper. Her argument is narrow and hard: a man who calls himself an anarchist while holding that women are a lesser order of being has contradicted himself, and one of the two claims has to go. She does not say which one. Whether Vázquez answered her a second time, the pages consulted do not show.
stops.quote: if they are anarchists, they cannot be for real, and if they are for real, they are no anarchists.
stops.quote_source: Lucía Sánchez Saornil, 'La cuestión femenina en nuestros medios,' Solidaridad Obrera, autumn 1935, trans. Paul Sharkey
sources: libcom.org, translation of the 1935 series by Paul Sharkey
suggested_refs: Mariano R. Vázquez's articles on women's liberation in the CNT press, 1935

stops.name: Paseo de Santa María de la Cabeza, Madrid, the magazine
stops.date_confidence: the first number of the magazine is attested for May 1936 and the Madrid agrupación for the same year; es.wikipedia's Mujeres Libres article dates the founding to April 1936, while English Wikipedia dates the organisation to 1937. The contradiction is left standing and not silently reconciled. The Paseo de Santa María de la Cabeza is attested as a family address from the 1910s to 1937; that the organisation was founded from her flat is an inference, and no house number is sourced. Issue count is also disputed: the Mujeres Libres article says fourteen, the Sánchez Saornil article numbers 1 to 13.
stops.campa: The first number of Mujeres Libres comes off the press in May, made by Sánchez Saornil, Mercedes Comaposada the lawyer and Amparo Poch y Gascón the doctor. Its programme is the ending of what they call the triple enslavement of women: to ignorance, to their sex, and to work. It is not a suffrage magazine and it is not a charity. Between the three of them they have a lawyer's training, a doctor's, and twenty years of getting into print past editors who would not have printed a woman. Thirteen issues appear before the war closes it, with a fourteenth set and never distributed.
stops.quote: Mujeres Libres is not interested in 'feminine unity,' because that does not represent anything.
stops.quote_source: Lucía Sánchez Saornil, quoted in Martha Ackelsberg, Free Women of Spain (AK Press)
suggested_refs: Mujeres Libres, issues 1-13 (Madrid and Barcelona, 1936-1938)

stops.name: Cuartel de la Montaña, Madrid, the barracks falls
stops.date_confidence: she is attested in the street on 19 July 1936 taking part in the assault; es.wikipedia's own account of the Madrid rising has the crowd besieging the barracks on the 19th and the storming taking place shortly before midday on the 20th, after artillery and air bombardment from Getafe. The stop is dated to the fall and the discrepancy is noted rather than resolved. The barracks stood where the Templo de Debod now stands.
stops.campa: The garrison of the Cuartel de la Montaña declares for the rising and the crowd comes for it, unarmed at first, then armed out of the Artillery Park. She is in that crowd on the nineteenth. Guns are brought up from Getafe, the walls are broken, and shortly before noon on the twentieth the barracks falls. Madrid stays Republican for two and a half more years. Within days she is filing as a war correspondent. Nothing of the barracks stands on the hill now; the Templo de Debod sits on the ground it held.
stops.quote: 19 July 1936! No other date is so full of meaning in the history of our people.
stops.quote_source: Lucía Sánchez Saornil, '19 July,' commemorative essay, translation republished by libcom.org
sources: Spanish Wikipedia, 'Golpe de Estado de julio de 1936 en Madrid'
suggested_refs: The site of the Cuartel de la Montaña, now the Templo de Debod, Madrid

stops.name: Barcelona, two organisations become one
stops.date_confidence: the merger of the Madrid Agrupación with Barcelona's Grupo Cultural Femenino is attested to 1936; the month orders the segment. The description of the capacitación programme is drawn from the general account of Mujeres Libres, not from a statement about her personally.
stops.campa: The Madrid agrupación joins with the Grupo Cultural Femenino of Barcelona, which has been organising Catalan working women since 1934, and the two halves become one body in two languages. She writes now for Solidaridad Obrera as well as for her own magazine. Reading and writing first, then trades, then driving and metalwork, with crèches so that mothers can attend. A woman who cannot read or feed herself is not free whatever the revolution has declared her to be. The organisation has a word for the whole programme: capacitación, the making of women capable.
suggested_refs: The Grupo Cultural Femenino of Barcelona, founded 1934

stops.name: Radio Madrid, Gran Vía, the poem under the bombardment
stops.date_confidence: attested to November 1936, the month of the assault on the capital; the day is not given. That the reading took place at the Gran Vía studios is a reconstruction from the location of Radio Madrid, not a sourced detail. Her readmission to Telefónica in October 1936 is attested separately by es.wikipedia and is mentioned here for the sequence.
stops.campa: Franco's columns reach the Casa de Campo and the capital is shelled from the ground and bombed from the air. Under the bombardment she writes 'Madrid, Madrid, mi Madrid' and reads it aloud over Radio Madrid. She is forty years old and back on the books of the company that let her go, readmitted in October with the workers running it. Twenty years at a switchboard and this is the first time the wire carries her own voice. Of the broadcast nothing survives: no recording, and no text of the poem in any source consulted. What Madrid heard that night is gone.
suggested_refs: Unión Radio Madrid broadcasts during the siege of Madrid, November 1936

stops.name: Valencia, Solidaridad Internacional Antifascista
stops.date_confidence: attested: sent by the CNT to Valencia in the spring of 1937, SIA founded in June 1937. She is secretary of press and propaganda of the Spanish section and editor-in-chief of the weekly Umbral, which she founds in the same period.
stops.campa: The CNT sends her to the wartime Republican capital in the spring to build an international relief organisation, and by June Solidaridad Internacional Antifascista exists: aid for the families of the dead, for refugees, for prisoners, run on libertarian principles and raising money abroad. She takes the press and propaganda desk of the Spanish section, and founds and edits the weekly Umbral, which will follow the government to Barcelona and stop in 1939. She is forty-one and has been getting words into print, under one name or another, for twenty-three years.
suggested_refs: Umbral, semanario de la nueva era (Valencia and Barcelona, 1937-1939)

stops.name: Valencia, the first national congress
stops.date_confidence: attested: the first national congress of Mujeres Libres opens in Valencia on 20 August 1937 with ninety local groups represented, and she becomes national secretary of the resulting federation. The figure of 147 agrupaciones belongs to 1938 and must not be read back to this date.
stops.campa: The first national congress of Mujeres Libres opens in Valencia on the twentieth of August. Ninety local groups send delegates, and the organisation constitutes itself as the Federación Nacional de Mujeres Libres with Sánchez Saornil as national secretary. It asks the CNT, the FAI and the Libertarian Youth to recognise it as a fourth branch of the libertarian movement, with a voice of its own in the movement's councils. It is refused, and the refusal is not reversed in the two years the federation has left.
stops.quote: This feminine force that we wish to create and that we are creating has, of course, a purpose and a political destiny much greater than sewing uniforms for militiamen or visiting the sick.
stops.quote_source: Lucía Sánchez Saornil, quoted in Martha Ackelsberg, Free Women of Spain (AK Press)
sources: Spanish Wikipedia, 'Mujeres Libres' (congress of 20 August 1937, ninety groups)
suggested_refs: Acts of the first national congress of Mujeres Libres, Valencia, August 1937

stops.name: Valencia, América Barroso
stops.date_confidence: 1937 attested for the meeting; the month is not given and orders the segment. The relationship is described in the sources as lifelong partnership; no self-description by either woman is quoted in the material consulted.
stops.campa: América Barroso García, called Mery, is working in the relief offices in Valencia. They meet in the middle of a war and stay together thirty-three years, through the border, the beach camp, the occupation, the clandestine return and twenty-two years in a Valencia flat behind a story about cousins. Mery is at the desk in 1937, on the road in 1939, at the sickbed in 1970. Nothing in the record is a declaration. No self-description by either woman survives in the material consulted, and what they called each other is not known.
suggested_refs: América Barroso García (Mery) in the SIA records, Valencia, 1937-1938

stops.name: Valencia, international secretary of SIA
stops.date_confidence: May 1938 attested for the appointment as international general secretary of SIA. The figures of 147 agrupaciones and roughly 20,000 members are attested for 1938, the 20,000 dated to October 1938 in the Mujeres Libres article. Romancero de Mujeres Libres is attested for 1938; its place of publication is not given in the sources consulted and it is treated here at her own posting rather than pinned elsewhere.
stops.campa: She is made international general secretary of SIA, running relief across a border that will shortly run the other way. Mujeres Libres now counts a hundred and forty-seven local groups and something near twenty thousand members, the largest organisation of working-class women Spain has ever had, built in two and a half years by three women with a magazine. The same year she publishes Romancero de Mujeres Libres. It is the only collection of her poetry to appear in her lifetime, and no source consulted names the city that printed it.
suggested_refs: Romancero de Mujeres Libres (1938)

stops.name: Barcelona, the Casal de la Dona Treballadora is cleared
stops.date_confidence: the eviction of the Casal and its transfer to the Bank of Spain building are attested for December 1938 by English Wikipedia; es.wikipedia does not date it. The protest letter to the CNT national committee is attested for 1938 via Ackelsberg; the original letter has not been consulted directly.
stops.campa: Police clear the Casal de la Dona Treballadora, the Barcelona school where thousands of women have been taught to read, to drive, to work metal, and the building is handed over to the Bank of Spain. She writes to the national committee of the CNT. The letter is polite, and it asks for little beyond an admission that Mujeres Libres exists and has done something worth knowing about. No reply from the committee is recorded. Two months later the Catalan front collapses and there is no committee left to write to.
stops.quote: It is a pity that you compañeros have always had so little time to acquaint yourselves with the valuable work of Mujeres Libres and that the consequence of this is the little interest you have shown in responding to our plea.
stops.quote_source: Lucía Sánchez Saornil, letter to the CNT national committee, 1938, quoted in Martha Ackelsberg, Free Women of Spain
sources: Martha Ackelsberg, Free Women of Spain (AK Press)
suggested_refs: The Casal de la Dona Treballadora, Barcelona, 1937-1938

stops.name: The Catalan border, out of Spain
stops.date_confidence: attested to January 1939 with the fall of Catalonia, in the company of América Barroso, Mateo Baruta and Cristina Kong; the exact crossing point and day are not given, and the coordinate is the general Cerdanya-Vallespir frontier. English Wikipedia dates her flight into France to February 1939 instead; the two accounts are left standing against each other.
stops.campa: Catalonia falls and half a million people walk north through the winter, the Retirada, and she is among them with Mery, Mateo Baruta and Cristina Kong. She is forty-three. She carries out of Spain a card in a union that no longer has a country, the national secretaryship of a federation of twenty thousand women that is about to be a crime, and a body of poetry that exists almost entirely in magazines nobody will ever bind. France is not expecting them and does not want them.
suggested_refs: The Retirada of January-February 1939 across the Pyrenean frontier

stops.name: Argelès-sur-Mer, the beach, and then Perpignan
stops.date_confidence: the brief internment at Argelers is attested by English Wikipedia and dated February 1939; es.wikipedia does not mention it and instead has her organising refugee distribution from Perpignan. The two accounts of her first weeks in France are not reconciled here. Coordinates for the camp vary by about half a kilometre between the sources consulted, and the Perpignan work is placed after the camp rather than before, against one source's ordering.
stops.campa: The French authorities pen the Spanish refugees on the sand between the sea and a line of wire, with no barracks, no latrines, nothing between them and the tramontane, and call it a concentration camp, which is their own word for it. Something like a hundred thousand people are on that beach. She is held there briefly and got out, and by the spring she is at Perpignan organising the distribution of the people still arriving. Two accounts of these weeks survive and they do not agree on the order.
suggested_refs: The camp at Argelès-sur-Mer, February 1939

stops.name: Paris, the relief machinery of a lost cause
stops.date_confidence: attested that her relief work for Spanish refugees continues in the region around Paris in 1939; the month is not given and is set to order the segment. That the outbreak of the European war coincides with her arrival is chronology, not a sourced connection.
stops.campa: She moves up to the outskirts of Paris and keeps the relief machinery turning: SIA still exists, in ledgers and letterheads, for a cause that has already lost its war. Spain is Franco's, the CNT is decapitated, Mujeres Libres is illegal. Her job is what it was in Valencia, moving money and food and papers to people behind wire, except that the war it belonged to is over and lost. On the first of September Germany invades Poland, and France is at war two days later.
suggested_refs: SIA relief operations for Spanish refugees in France, 1939

stops.name: Orléans, España Expatriada
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. es.wikipedia carries her direction of the weekly España Expatriada from Orléans without a firm date; the month here orders the segment, and coordinates for Orléans vary slightly between the sources consulted.
stops.campa: From Orléans she directs a weekly called España Expatriada, which is exactly what the title says: a paper for a country that has become a diaspora scattered through French internment camps. It is her fourth periodical, and Mery is with her; the two of them have been in France close on a year. She is editing for readers behind wire, in a language the host country does not print in, about a defeat none of them have finished absorbing. The sources give no run, no print figure, no single issue date. What survives of the paper is its title.
stops.quote: We know that 19 July continues to burn within us, shining in the darkness of our torture as the only hope.
stops.quote_source: Lucía Sánchez Saornil, '19 July,' commemorative essay, translation republished by libcom.org
suggested_refs: España Expatriada (Orléans), the exile weekly

stops.name: Montauban, the unoccupied south
stops.date_confidence: attested: the move to Montauban follows the French collapse and is dated to June 1940 by es.wikipedia. Mery's work with a Quaker organisation and Sánchez Saornil's photographic retouching at home are attested for this period.
stops.campa: France falls in six weeks and the exiles move again, south, into the unoccupied zone. In Montauban Mery finds work with a Quaker relief organisation and Lucía retouches photographs at home for money. The national secretary of the Federación Nacional de Mujeres Libres sits in a rented room in the Tarn-et-Garonne painting shadows back into other people's portraits by hand. There is no organisation left to be secretary of. The mail is read. They stay two years.
suggested_refs: Spanish Republican exile communities at Montauban, 1940-1942

stops.name: Montauban, the letters opened
stops.date_confidence: es.wikipedia carries a late-1941 notice pressing the two women toward a forced albergue and, separately, a brief arrest over suspicious correspondence in early 1942; these are distinct events and the arrest belongs to 1942. English Wikipedia instead has her escaping arrest ahead of a planned deportation and dates it loosely to the occupation. The accounts are left unreconciled.
stops.campa: Late in 1941 a notice presses the two of them toward a forced labour shelter; early in 1942 they are briefly arrested over correspondence the authorities find suspicious. Vichy is deporting foreign nationals and Spanish Republicans are on the lists. So she makes the calculation: Franco's Spain, where she is a known anarchist, a known editor and a woman living with another woman, is now the safer of the two countries. The Spanish and English accounts of that arrest do not agree with each other.
suggested_refs: Vichy internment and deportation policy toward Spanish Republicans, 1941-1942

stops.name: La Jonquera, back across
stops.date_confidence: March 1942 attested for the clandestine return with the help of Electra, América Barroso's sister; the crossing point at La Jonquera follows from the geography of the return rather than from an explicit statement in the sources, and the day is not given.
stops.campa: They cross back at La Jonquera in March, helped by Electra, Mery's sister, whose papers are good where theirs are not. Nobody at the post is looking for a middle-aged woman travelling with her cousin. She has been out of Spain three years and one month. Everything she made before the border, the magazine, the federation, the ninety delegates and then the hundred and forty-seven groups, is now a thing that will get her shot if it is attached to her name. So the name goes.
suggested_refs: Clandestine returns of Spanish exiles across the Catalan frontier, 1942

stops.name: Calle de Donoso Cortés, Madrid, the lease
stops.date_confidence: the lease on Calle de Donoso Cortés is attested for July 1942 and the padrón entry for 1945, folded here into one stop. Correction: she is not recorded as living under a false name. The fiction in the record is that Mery is entered as her cousin. Her occupations in these years, comisionista and hairnet maker, are attested.
stops.campa: In July she signs a lease in Chamberí and begins again as a nobody. She works as a commission agent and makes hairnets. In the census of 1945 she is entered as head of household with Mery beside her, described as her cousin, and that is the whole of the disguise, and it holds for the rest of both their lives. There is no forged identity in the record and no false name. There is one wrong word, cousin, and thirty years of nobody looking twice. The lease is in her own name.
stops.quote: But 19 July continues to triumph as the only truth and the only way out.
stops.quote_source: Lucía Sánchez Saornil, '19 July,' commemorative essay, translation republished by libcom.org
sources: Spanish Wikipedia, 'Lucía Sánchez Saornil' (lease July 1942; padrón of 1945)
suggested_refs: The Madrid padrón of 1945, Calle de Donoso Cortés

stops.name: Madrid, the manifesto of 1946
stops.date_confidence: the 1946 manifesto is documented flatly by es.wikipedia; the reconstruction tag applies to how far the clandestine reorganisation of Mujeres Libres actually went, not to the existence of the document. Her attendance at clandestine confederal meetings is reported without detail. Month not given, defaulted.
stops.campa: A manifesto from 1946 survives, and she is seen at clandestine confederal meetings in the capital. Whether Mujeres Libres was genuinely being rebuilt under the dictatorship, or whether a handful of women were writing to each other and calling it that, the record does not settle. What is certain is that four years after crossing back she is not finished, in a country where the sentence for what she is doing is death. Two years later she leaves Madrid.
sources: Spanish Wikipedia, 'Lucía Sánchez Saornil' (1946 manifesto; clandestine meetings)
suggested_refs: The Mujeres Libres manifesto of 1946

stops.name: Russafa, Valencia, the flat
stops.date_confidence: January 1948 attested for the move to Valencia, into a flat provided by Elena Samada, Mery's niece. Coordinates corrected to Russafa proper; several sources carry a value about half a kilometre northwest, nearer the Estació del Nord. The knitwear business Gabriren and the private lessons are attested.
stops.campa: Repression tightens and they leave the capital for a flat in Russafa given them by Mery's niece, Elena Samada. She opens a small business called Gabriren, representing knitwear, and gives private lessons on the side. Twenty-one years earlier the telephone company had posted her to this same city on service requirements, for reasons that had nothing to do with anything. The neighbours know a commission agent who keeps to herself. She is fifty-two. She will not leave Valencia again.
suggested_refs: The barrio of Russafa, Valencia, in the first Franco decades

stops.name: Valencia, the identity card
stops.date_confidence: June 1953 attested for the issue of her first Spanish national identity document since the exile, with the profession entered as fan painter. The day is not given, and the issuing office is not identified in the sources.
stops.campa: Eleven years after the return the state issues her a national identity document, the first it has put her name on since the war. The profession printed on it is pintora de abanicos, fan painter. The same state would have shot the national secretary of the Federación Nacional de Mujeres Libres. She had studied painting at the Casa de los Gatos forty years earlier, which makes the entry not quite a lie. The card is issued in Valencia in June; which office issued it the sources do not say.
suggested_refs: Spanish Documento Nacional de Identidad records, Valencia, June 1953

stops.name: Burgos, the poem in Estrofa
stops.date_confidence: October 1955 attested for the publication of 'Quiero en mi ley cumplirme' in Estrofa, described by es.wikipedia as a Falangist youth magazine published in Burgos. She is living in Valencia; the pin marks where the poem is printed, not where she stands. Whether the editors knew whose verse they were setting is not established anywhere consulted.
stops.campa: A magazine of the Falangist youth, printed in Burgos, runs a poem of hers called 'Quiero en mi ley cumplirme,' which means, roughly, let me be fulfilled according to my own law. She had argued against the coming order in this city twenty-two years before. The organ of the movement that won prints her verse, and the record does not say whether anyone in the office knew what they were setting. It is one of very few poems she is known to have published in the twenty-eight years between the border and her death.
suggested_refs: Estrofa, revista burgalesa de la juventud falangista, October 1955

stops.name: Russafa, Valencia, the last poems
stops.date_confidence: the manuscript collection of late poems is dated to around 1960 by es.wikipedia; the literary gatherings in Russafa through the 1950s and 1960s are a reconstruction from the general account rather than a dated event. The London founding of the exile federation in December 1963 is attested; she is not connected to it, and it is named here as what happens to her organisation without her.
stops.campa: She keeps writing. A body of poetry accumulates in the flat, unpublished and signed with no pseudonym because there is no editor left to hide from, and small gatherings meet in Russafa where she reads aloud to a few people who know her as a retired commission agent. In December 1963, in London, the surviving militants of Mujeres Libres constitute a federation in exile and start a bulletin that will run to forty-seven issues. She is in Russafa, and she is not among them.
sources: Spanish Wikipedia, 'Mujeres Libres' (Federación de Mujeres Libres de España en el Exilio, London, December 1963)
suggested_refs: The bulletin of the Federación de Mujeres Libres de España en el Exilio, 1964-1976

stops.name: Valencia, the death
stops.date_confidence: attested to 2 June 1970, of breast cancer, aged seventy-four, four months after the death of her sister Concha. That no obituary appeared is a reconstruction from the conditions, not a sourced statement.
stops.campa: Her sister Concha dies in February. She dies of breast cancer on the second of June, seventy-four years old, in the city she came to in order to vanish into it. The neighbours bury a woman who represented knitwear. There is no one in Spain permitted to print what she was: the poet Luciano de San-Saor, the editor of Umbral, national secretary of twenty thousand organised women, the voice that read a poem over Radio Madrid under the bombs. She is buried two days later.
suggested_refs: Valencia civil death register, 2 June 1970

stops.name: Cementerio General de Valencia, the stone
stops.date_confidence: the inscription chosen by América Barroso is attested verbatim by es.wikipedia, which prints it without an opening inverted question mark. The burial date is not given and 4 June orders the segment. Coordinates corrected to the Cementerio General de Valencia; several sources carry a value about four kilometres north of the true site. Mery died of a heart attack in 1977; that she was interred in the same tomb is repeated but not sourced in the material consulted.
stops.campa: Mery has a line of Lucía's own verse cut into the stone: Pero... es verdad que la esperanza ha muerto? But is it true that hope has died? It is a question and it is left as one, on a grave in a country where the answer, in 1970, is not seriously in doubt. No organisation is named on the stone and no dates appear but the two. For twenty-six years almost nobody comes to it, and the name cut above the line means nothing to the city it stands in. Mery lives another seven years and dies of a heart attack in 1977.
stops.quote: Pero... es verdad que la esperanza ha muerto?
stops.quote_source: The inscription chosen by América Barroso for the grave, Cementerio General de Valencia, a line from Sánchez Saornil's own poetry
suggested_refs: The Cementerio General de Valencia, Calle Santo Domingo de Guzmán 27

stops.name: Valencia, the poems come back
stops.date_confidence: attested: Poesía (Pre-Textos, 1996), edited by Rosa Martín Casamitjana, is the first posthumous gathering; Corcel de fuego (2020) is edited by Nuria Capdevila-Argüelles; the critical edition of the late manuscripts, Siempre puede volver la esperanza (Fundación Emilio Hurtado, 2022), is edited with introduction and notes by Jesús Gallego Montero. A widely repeated credit to a researcher named Michela Cimbalo for the recovery is not corroborated in the sources consulted and is not asserted. Months are not given.
stops.campa: Twenty-six years after the burial, Pre-Textos publishes Poesía, the first gathering of the work of Luciano de San-Saor under the name of the woman who wrote it. Corcel de fuego follows in 2020 with the poems of 1914 to 1931. The manuscripts left in the Russafa flat appear in 2022 as Siempre puede volver la esperanza, hope can always return, which reads like an answer given back to the stone. Her war journalism is reprinted in 2019, and the Solidaridad Obrera articles in 2016.
sources: Spanish Wikipedia, 'Lucía Sánchez Saornil' (Poesía 1996; Corcel de fuego 2020; Siempre puede volver la esperanza 2022; Horas de revolución reprint 2019; La cuestión femenina en nuestros medios 2016)
suggested_refs: Poesía, ed. Rosa Martín Casamitjana (Pre-Textos, 1996)

stops.name: San Blas-Canillejas, Madrid, the name on the door
stops.date_confidence: attested: the Espacio de Igualdad Lucía Sánchez Saornil opened in the San Blas-Canillejas district of Madrid in 2019, month not given; the Correos commemorative stamp is attested for September 2023; an annual homage at her grave in Valencia in early June is attested as recurring, with no fixed year.
stops.campa: Madrid puts her name on the door of a municipal equality centre in San Blas-Canillejas, a district built long after she left the city. In September 2023 the Spanish post office prints her face on a stamp; she was photographed so rarely during the war that the scarcity of images is part of how she survived it. The city of the Peñuelas and the switchboard carries her name the ordinary municipal way now, on a building with opening hours. Every year, in the first days of June, a small group gathers at the grave in Valencia.
sources: Spanish Wikipedia, 'Lucía Sánchez Saornil' (Espacio de Igualdad, 2019; Correos stamp, September 2023; annual homage)
suggested_refs: Espacio de Igualdad Lucía Sánchez Saornil, San Blas-Canillejas, Madrid
